events.feedback:
As someone who works with palms and public collections daily, scanning this QR code in the field gives a solid foundation, but a few key tweaks in tone, focus, and botanical nuance will make it hit harder for a curious visitor.

Here is honest feedback on what works, what needs fixing, and how to dial in the voice.

What Left Me Confined, Missing, or Plain Wrong

Missing—The Water Paradox Needs Context: You hit hard that it’s a riverbank plant, but visitors will look around Palma Sola (or a home yard) and see it living in regular soil. Explain how it manages that. It isn't an aquatic plant that dies if it leaves standing water; it’s an opportunistic root-grower that tolerates high water tables but starves for oxygen and nutrients when shoved into tight pot soil or high-alkalinity Florida sand.

events.summary: Corrected IUCN status from Vulnerable to Endangered throughout; added hydrochory as the wild seed-dispersal mechanism in the Fruit block; sharpened prose in quick_hits, more_information, and other_notes per reviewer direction (active voice, visitor-facing 'water paradox' explanation, cleaner hook); simplified the Flowers block to what a visitor standing 5 feet away can see; added a staff-fill note for male/female specimen status; updated seasonality notes to reflect male/female visitor prompt.

events.feedback:
Yes. This is much closer to the kind of page that could make a botanist or palm person stop and read, but if I were visiting Palma Sola as someone from Selby or a palm collection, I'd have a pretty strong reaction:
“You clearly did your homework. But you've found several genuinely excellent stories here, and then buried them under a lot of horticultural detail—and a few claims I'd want you to tighten before I put my name behind the page.”
I checked the species against current botanical/conservation sources while reading it. Kew currently accepts Ravenea rivularis and gives its native range as southwestern Madagascar. The conservation story is real and very good, although there are some important nuances in how you present it.
My overall reaction
The conservation + river habitat story is the killer feature of this palm.
You have, potentially, a terrific three-part story:
This is the palm you see everywhere in garden centers.
In nature, it is an extremely restricted Madagascar river palm
events.summary: Applied reviewer's comprehensive restructuring: built the page around the endangered river-palm story rather than horticultural detail, eliminated the butterfly section, cut the fertilizer and stress-signaling paragraphs, qualified the 900-tree figure to the IUCN assessment, removed the unverifiable Ravené etymology, added Ravenea genus context, simplified the safety note, tightened the 'what to look for' closing, and pruned the river-habitat repetition that appeared across six fields.

events.feedback:
Regarding the staff note in the Notes section, you write: [STAFF NOTE: Confirm the sex of the specimen(s) at this location and update this sign accordingly. If a female is present and fruiting, note it explicitly so visitors can make the connection in real time.]

Consider this: very botanical garden in the world labels species without sexing each plant, because for most palms you cannot know until it flowers — which can take a decade or more, and a juvenile Majesty Palm in a pot is simply unsexable.

What creates the itch isn't the omission, it's leaving the obvious question hanging. A visitor reads "male and female on separate trees," looks up, and wants to know which. One sentence closes it without a single field hour:

You can only tell when it flowers or fruits — a fruiting tree is female.
